cards.front: Which part of an amino acid varies, giving twenty different amino acids?
cards.back: The **R group** is the variable side group on the central carbon. Its differences change how the protein folds and what it can do.
cards.hint: Think about the four groups attached to the central carbon.

cards.front: How does a peptide bond form between two amino acids?
cards.back: The **carboxyl group** of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the other, releasing a molecule of water. This is a condensation reaction.
cards.hint: Start by identifying which two groups react.

cards.front: Why can changing one amino acid in a chain change a protein's final shape?
cards.back: The primary structure sets which R groups sit at which positions. Those R groups control how the chain folds, so the sequence decides every higher level.
cards.hint: Consider what decides which R groups interact with each other.

cards.front: Which bonds hold the secondary structure together, and what shapes does it form?
cards.back: **Hydrogen bonds** between oxygen in one peptide link and hydrogen in a nearby link form the alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet. Each bond is weak, but many together are stable.
cards.hint: Only the repeating part of the chain takes part here.

cards.front: What is the tertiary structure of a protein?
cards.back: The **tertiary structure** is the overall three-dimensional shape of one polypeptide, held by interactions between R groups.
A **disulfide bond** is a covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine R groups. It is stronger than a hydrogen bond.
cards.hint: Think about which amino acid contains sulfur.

cards.front: Why do non-polar R groups cluster inside a folded protein?
cards.back: They pack away from water inside the protein, forming a hydrophobic interaction that helps hold the tertiary structure in place.
cards.hint: Think about how oily molecules behave in water.

cards.front: What is the quaternary structure of a protein?
cards.back: The **quaternary structure** is the arrangement of two or more polypeptides in one protein. Haemoglobin has four, joined mainly by the same kinds of bond as in tertiary structure.

cards.front: A student says hydrolysis releases water. Why is this wrong?
cards.back: Hydrolysis uses water to break a peptide bond. Condensation is the reaction that releases water when a bond forms.
cards.hint: Compare what happens to water in each reaction.

cards.front: A student says a protein made of one polypeptide has a quaternary structure. Why is this wrong?
cards.back: Quaternary structure needs two or more polypeptides in one protein. A protein with a single polypeptide has no quaternary structure.

cards.front: Which bonds hold the primary structure together?
cards.back: Only **peptide bonds** hold the primary structure together. The gene fixes the order of amino acids, so each protein has its own sequence.
cards.hint: Think about what joins amino acids in the first place.

cards.front: How do globular proteins differ in shape from fibrous proteins such as collagen?
cards.back: Globular proteins fold into compact shapes with hydrophobic R groups inside. Fibrous proteins like collagen are long and strong, with three polypeptides wound together.
cards.hint: Compare how compact each shape is.

cards.front: A student says the amino group is the acidic part of an amino acid. What is wrong?
cards.back: The **carboxyl group** is the acidic part. The amino group contains nitrogen and is not the acidic group.
cards.hint: Check which group the note describes as acidic.
